reviewed: CODEX_MASTER_PROMPT.md v1.0 (2026-09-23), Parts D and R in full, and the parts of A, C, E, H and N that touch them; compared line by line with the forge's reviewed parts/D_control_plane_dashboard_migration.md and parts/R_resilience_failsafes.md; checked against research-data/infra/infra_facts_tooling.json, research-data/probe/results_2026-09-23/gpu_probe_2026-09-23.json, 00_README.md and 00_REQUEST_PROMPT.md

findings.where: R.2 (worker unit, 'Pause on the lab', emergency stop, transient scopes); D.1 ('Pause is always safe'; 'stop with the worker'); D.2 emergency_stop; I6; N.10
findings.problem: Packed jobs run in transient scopes (systemd-run --user --scope --slice=smatsprint-exp.slice), which are separate units from smatsprint-worker.service. KillMode=mixed sends the final SIGKILL only to the worker unit's own cgroup, and 'systemctl --user kill --signal=SIGKILL smatsprint-worker.service' reaches only that cgroup too. The adaptation still says 'anything still alive at TimeoutStopSec=50 is killed' (R.2) and 'the environment processes are in the same slice and stop with the worker' (D.1). It dropped the forge's sentence that made Pause work ('the main worker process, not systemd, stops those scopes at the grace limit'). With 32-48 single-threaded environment processes per job, jobs get 45 s and the worker must stop every scope and exit inside TimeoutStopSec=50, which leaves 5 s. Verification snapshots PIDs before the signal. That misses processes spawned after the snapshot, and C.5 reads desired.json only at start, not before each admission. Under cgroup v2 a slice's own cgroup.procs is empty, so a literal implementation verifies nothing. N.10 registers no need for a Pause that fails to verify (the forge had pause_not_verified). The forge's R.2 still has the emergency-stop and crash-restart variants of this gap. Report that to the user; do not touch the forge.
findings.scenario: (a) Emergency stop kills the worker's main process. Every trainer and its 48 environment processes keep running in their scopes, while the banner says PAUSED and the GPU and 48 cores stay busy. (b) One job is slow to tear down its environments. At 50 s systemd SIGKILLs the worker, and the job's scope is orphaned. (c) The worker crashes, is OOM-killed or gets a watchdog SIGABRT. Restart=on-failure restarts it with the same epoch, because a systemd restart does not pass through the controller. The new worker resumes every job in running/ while the old job processes are still alive, so two writers share one run directory and its checkpoints. (d) The controller writes run=false, and the still-running worker admits one more job in the next second. That job's 48 environment processes are not in the snapshot.
findings.fix: Replace the R.2 clause 'anything still alive at TimeoutStopSec=50 is killed and resumes from its last checkpoint' and the D.1 sentence 'Pause also frees the CPU cores: the environment processes are in the same slice and stop with the worker' with: 'Job scopes are separate units, so stopping or killing the worker unit does not reach them. (1) Each scope is created with -p BindsTo=smatsprint-worker.service -p After=smatsprint-worker.service -p TimeoutStopSec=40 (verify on systemd 255 in Phase 0; if refused, (2) and (3) are the guarantee) and is named smatsprint-job-<job_id>-<worker INVOCATION_ID>. (2) Every environment process sets prctl(PR_SET_PDEATHSIG, SIGKILL). Every trainer holds an exclusive flock on runs/<job_id>/.lock for its lifetime and refuses to start without it. (3) At every worker start, before resuming anything, the worker stops every smatsprint-job-* scope whose invocation id is not its own. (4) The worker re-reads desired.json before every admission and before spawning processes. (5) Pause = systemctl --user stop smatsprint-worker.service, then systemctl --user stop smatsprint-exp.slice. Emergency stop = write 1 to the slice cgroup.kill, then stop the slice. (6) Pause is verified when smatsprint-exp.slice/cgroup.events reads populated 0 and, on two nvidia-smi reads 2 s apart, no GPU PID has a cgroup under smatsprint.slice (except a permitted viewer, SM-11). If that has not happened 55 s after the command, write cgroup.kill. If the slice is still populated at 75 s, raise pause_not_verified with the PIDs and an Emergency stop button.' Change I6 to 'after Pause is acknowledged, smatsprint-exp.slice holds no process and no GPU process belongs to it'. Add pause_not_verified to N.10.
findings.test: Integration (gates M1): a dummy job ignores SIGTERM for 120 s and forks 48 busy-looping children inside its scope. (a) Pause leaves cgroup.events at populated 0 within 60 s. (b) Emergency stop does so within 5 s. (c) kill -9 of only the worker's main process: systemd restarts the worker, the stale scope is stopped before any resume, the job never runs twice (the lock), and its parameters equal a never-killed twin's. (d) A job admitted in the 1 s between the desired.json write and SIGTERM never spawns. (e) A leftover scope holding a fake nvidia-smi PID blocks verification and raises pause_not_verified.

findings.where: D.2 'Epoch fencing'; D.2 lab_mirror, move_to_lab, Park; D.1 job delivery rule; C.5 worker resume; H.5 'Pause / resume a candidate'
findings.problem: 'The mirror, the record copier and the moves ignore anything with an older epoch' contradicts resume. Every worker start increments worker_epoch, so every checkpoint a worker resumes from is older by construction. The rule also rejects legitimate files that never get a newer stamp: checkpoints of candidates paused through H.5 ('a running job checkpoints and stops'), jobs in running/ that were not re-admitted after a restart because RAM, GPU or disk admission failed, and a DONE written just before an epoch bump that the 60 s record copier has not yet pulled. The delivery rule re-delivers a job only if it is 'absent from all four worker-side queue directories and from record/'. A DONE that the copier ignores therefore leaves the job in done/, unrecorded and undeliverable forever. The forge's D.2 has the same wording, and this programme's per-candidate pause makes the case common.
findings.scenario: On Vast the user pauses candidate C. Later, a user Pause and Resume and a guard restart raise the epoch twice, while C's checkpoint still carries the old epoch. lab_mirror skips it, and move_to_lab verifies only current-epoch files, swaps, and destroys the instance at step 5. C's progress on Vast is gone. Separately, SSH to Vast drops for 3 minutes just after job J writes DONE, and the user presses Pause then Resume, so the epoch moves on. The copier then ignores J's DONE, J never enters record/, and the pipeline waiting on J (S2 after S1) stalls with no alert.
findings.fix: Replace the last sentence of 'Epoch fencing' with: 'Fencing is by lineage, not by order. state/epochs.jsonl records every worker start {epoch, host, lease_id, started_at} and every fence {host, lease_id, at}: a replacement, a destroy under the I2 unreachable clause, or a to_destroy lease. A file read from a host is accepted when its worker_epoch was issued to that host, or to an earlier unfenced host of the same lineage. It is rejected when its epoch belongs to a fenced host or lease, or is newer than the current epoch. Resume, the mirror, the record copier and every covering copy use this one predicate. Checkpoints of paused candidates and of jobs not yet re-admitted are part of every covering copy. If the record copier must reject a DONE or FAILED, the controller moves that job out of the worker-side done/ into failed/ with reason fenced in the same step, so no job is ever both unrecorded and undeliverable.' Add I11: 'every delivered job is eventually either recorded or re-deliverable'.
findings.test: Model plus integration (gates M2 and M5). (1) Pause a candidate on a fake Vast host, cycle the worker twice, then run move_to_lab: the candidate's checkpoint is copied, verified and resumes. (2) Write DONE, block SSH for 3 minutes, pause and resume, then unblock: exactly one record and no stranded job. (3) A fenced host returning with older-epoch files contributes nothing. (4) A stateful property test over random interleavings: I11 holds after every step.

findings.where: D.1 ('also move the sandbox'); D.2 move_to_vast step 4, move_to_lab, destroy_vast, evacuate_vast_to_drive, lease_cap, parked_destroy, Replace, copies.sandbox, backup_covers_stop, I2; D.7 ('archived only if ticked'); H.4 layers 1, 4, 6, 7; H.7; H.11 LI1
findings.problem: The user asked for the tick-box ('The sandbox lane travels with the experiment lane on a move only if I tick it'), and also wrote 'When I move from Vast back to the GPU server, everything moves back' and 'Nothing is deleted before its replacement copy is verified'. Only move_to_vast mentions the sandbox. No path brings it back before a destroy: move_to_lab step 5, destroy_vast, evacuate_vast_to_drive (unless a separate tick is set), the lease_cap come-home, parked_destroy and fence-first replace all omit it. backup_covers_stop and I2 cover the experiment only. lab_mirror mirrors experiment checkpoints only. copies.sandbox has no generation, verification or age. Every lane-separation layer is lab-only. bubblewrap usually cannot create namespaces in an unprivileged Docker container. A container has no systemd slices for the CPU and RAM fence. The inotify and cgroup watcher runs on the lab. The idle stop, the sandbox queue and the viewer tunnel ('ssh -L 8801 … sail-gpu') all assume the lab. On Vast the sandbox and the experiment work tree share one user in one container, and that work tree returns to the lab through move_to_lab, trusted after a manifest check that a same-user process can forge. The lab's copy of the sandbox and the Vast copy can also diverge.
findings.scenario: The user ticks 'also move the sandbox' and works on Vast for two days. A lease cap triggers come-home: move_to_lab step 5 destroys the instance and two days of sandbox configs, runs and clips with it. No dialog warns, because backup_covers_stop is true for the experiment. Or a sandbox script on Vast rewrites work/runs/<id>/ckpt/ and its manifest for a running experiment job. No watcher sees it, and the result comes back to the lab labelled EXPERIMENT, breaking A.5 rule 12 and LI1.
findings.fix: Keep the tick-box, as the user asked, and specify it end to end. D.1: 'When ticked, the sandbox tree moves as a second work state, sbx.d/<generation>/ behind a sandbox symlink. It uses the same staging, verification and one-rename swap as work/, and has its own manifest (sandbox runs keep checkpoint manifests like experiment runs) and copies.sandbox = {where, generation, verified_at, covers_stop}.' D.2: 'move_to_lab, destroy_vast, evacuate_vast_to_drive, lease_cap (both outcomes), parked_destroy and fence-first replace each copy the sandbox tree back and verify it before any stop or destroy. backup_covers_stop becomes {exp, sbx}, and I2 requires both, or the typed word DELETE-SANDBOX in the dialog. lab_mirror also mirrors pinned sandbox checkpoints. While the sandbox is away, the lab sandbox tree is a read-only backup, and sprintctl sbx on the lab refuses runs and points at Vast.' H.4 on Vast: 'The sandbox runs as a separate Unix user, sbx, created in the container, and the experiment work tree is mode 0700 for the worker's user, so Unix permissions enforce LI1 there. Use bwrap only if the rehearsal shows it works in the container. The supervisor enforces the sandbox thread cap and the VRAM watchdog. The idle stop and the sandbox queue run under the supervisor. The viewer is reached by a double tunnel through the lab, documented in the guide and tested. Promote requests from Vast are pulled into staging as untrusted data.' The tick-box stays disabled, with the reason, until each of these passes the rehearsal.
findings.test: State-machine model: with the sandbox on Vast, every path to destroy (move_to_lab, destroy_vast, evacuate_vast_to_drive, lease_cap, parked_destroy, replace) either copies the sandbox back verified or is refused. On the rehearsal instance, the lanes fuzzer runs as the sbx user and cannot create, modify or delete anything under the work tree. A guide test runs the double-tunnel viewer command.

findings.where: D.3 'Ordering and staleness' ('At most one transition command is in progress; another is rejected with busy')
findings.problem: The forge's D.3 exempted pause, emergency_stop, cancel_move, settings and register_device from busy rejection. The adaptation dropped that exemption. As written, Pause and Emergency stop are refused during any move, backup or restore. cancel_move exists only during a transition, so it can never run. This contradicts D.2 'Pause never abandons a transition' and the definition of cancel_move. Automatic safety transitions are not addressed either: a polite_pause during an hour-long backup_to_drive, or a lease_cap during a Drive refresh on Vast, would be busy-rejected.
findings.scenario: A 40-minute move_to_lab is copying. A lab mate needs the machine, the user presses Emergency stop, and the answer is 'busy: move_to_lab'. Or a lab mate starts a GPU job during backup_to_drive, polite_pause is busy-rejected, and the experiment keeps the GPU for the rest of the backup.
findings.fix: Append to the D.3 sentence: 'except pause, stop, emergency_stop, cancel_move, settings, register_device and the automatic polite_pause and lease_cap, which are never busy-rejected. pause and emergency_stop during a transition set transition.end_phase=PAUSED (D.2). cancel_move runs the rollback. A polite_pause during a move is already satisfied by the move's step 1; during backup_to_drive it stops the worker, and the archive reads a pinned snapshot (SM-20). A lease_cap during a Drive operation on Vast pre-empts it; the Drive operation resumes after the park.'
findings.test: State-machine model: inject each exempt command at every step of every transition. None is rejected with busy, and I1-I10 hold. Playwright: Pause and Emergency stop stay enabled during every transition.

findings.where: D.6 'Worker self-guard'; D.6 'Lease and billing' ('90 % alerts; 100 % runs lease_cap'); D.2 lease_cap; I8
findings.problem: (1) 'vastai stop instance $CONTAINER_ID' passes no key. The CLI resolves its key only from an argument, VAST_API_KEY, the XDG config file or ~/.vast_api_key (infra fact vast-11), and none exists on a credential-free worker, so the self-stop fails. (2) CONTAINER_API_KEY is a container environment variable, and a guard started or restarted over SSH during provisioning may not inherit it. (3) The guard stops at 90 % of the money cap, but the controller's lease_cap starts only at cost_so_far + dph × estimated_sync_hours ≥ 100 %. The fallback therefore always pre-empts the orderly path. It stops the instance with backup_covers_stop=false, the default at_cap=come_home_if_lab_free never runs, and every capped lease goes down the stopped-instance path. That path depends on a restart Vast may delay indefinitely, or on copying off a stopped instance, which the docs do not confirm to local (vast-13). (4) The adaptation dropped the forge's lower-bound cost formula, its 30-minute wait on state/sync_in_progress, its stop sequence, and its fallback for when the key cannot stop the instance. (5) The same key can destroy the instance (vast-10), and nothing forbids the guard from doing so.
findings.scenario: A USD 60 lease reaches USD 54 on a healthy lab. The guard stops the instance mid-job, and the lab never gets its orderly copy home. Or the lab goes silent for 6 h: the guard's 'vastai stop instance' fails authentication, and the instance bills until someone notices.
findings.fix: Replace the guard bullet with: 'Worker self-guard (ops/vast/worker_guard.py, its own process group, no user credentials, started by onstart and restartable over SSH). It reads CONTAINER_API_KEY and CONTAINER_ID from its environment, or from /proc/1/environ when absent, and never writes or logs them. It stops the instance only with vastai --api-key $CONTAINER_API_KEY stop instance $CONTAINER_ID and never calls destroy. Its cost is a lower bound computed from the lease file: dph × elapsed hours + storage_cost × disk GB × elapsed months. It stops when (a) that bound reaches 100 % of max_usd, after waiting at most 30 more minutes while a state/sync_in_progress stamp under 10 minutes old shows an orderly park; (b) the controller has been silent for lab_silence_stop_h; or (c) the queue has been empty and the controller silent for 30 minutes. Sequence: run=false, SIGTERM the worker groups, wait up to 45 s, sync, write stopped_by=guard and the reason to state/guard.log, then stop.' In D.2 lease_cap and D.6, change the controller's trigger to cost_so_far + dph × estimated_sync_hours ≥ 0.9 × max_usd, so the orderly path finishes first. Add: 'If the M5 rehearsal shows the key cannot stop the instance, record it in docs/PLAN.md, make max_hours a hard stop at 12 h through the controller, and rely on the dead-man alert.'
findings.test: Rehearsal (M5): kill the guard, restart it over SSH rather than by onstart, block the lab link, and confirm the self-stop works with only the container key. Fake-clock unit test: at 90 % the controller's park starts and completes before the guard acts; with the controller silent, the guard stops at 100 % of its bound. A grep test finds no 'destroy' in worker_guard.py.

findings.where: D.2 'Park' paragraph; D.2 lease_cap, Vast pause (park_after_min), destroy_vast; I8; D.2 lab_mirror no-room mode
findings.problem: The adaptation dropped the forge's definition of a 'full copy'. The forge counted each run's kept checkpoints per its manifest, the worker queue copied whole into staging and swapped by one rename, the base artefacts and every small file, hash-verified, and it named a verified Drive archive as the alternative when the lab has no room. It also dropped the forge's flag rules: any worker start on Vast sets the flag false, and a guard or Vast-side stop leaves it false. What remains orders parking, lease caps, destroy_vast, move_to_lab and evacuation as 'pause, full copy, verify, set backup_covers_stop, and only then stop or destroy'. When the lab is under its free-space floor, which A.4's measured 80-82 GB free makes likely, no covering copy is possible and no alternative is named. The stop never comes and the GPU bills past the cap, violating I8. Stopping never loses data, because a stopped instance keeps its disk. Only destroy needs the copy.
findings.scenario: The experiment is on Vast and the lab has 62 GB free, so the mirror is in results_only mode. The lease reaches its cap. Come-home is refused on disk, the park's 'full copy' to the lab is refused by the floor, and Drive is not a named target for a park. The instance keeps billing USD 0.47/h, while the dashboard says the cap holds.
findings.fix: Replace the Park paragraph with: 'A covering copy is the work state as move_to_lab step 2 copies it: every run's kept checkpoints per its manifest, paused candidates included; work/queue/ copied whole into staging and swapped by one rename, so no job is ever in two queue states; work/refdata/; and every small file, all hash-verified. It goes into the lab backup by the mirror's method when lab free space minus its size stays above the floor rule of SM-07, and otherwise into a verified Drive archive (D.7). backup_covers_stop is set only when a covering copy verifies after the worker's last exit. Any worker start on Vast sets it false, and a guard or Vast-side stop leaves it false. Destroy requires the flag or the I2 unreachable clause. Stop never waits for a copy. When a lease cap, the credit floor or park_after_min is reached and a covering copy cannot finish within one check interval, or is impossible, the instance is stopped at once and lease_cap_reached names both options. The data stays on the stopped disk, and the copy is made after the next start.'
findings.test: Model test with the lab below the floor, Drive too small and the lease at its cap: the instance is stopped within one 5-minute interval, never destroyed, and the need is raised. With room: copy, verify, set the flag, then stop, in that order. A guard stop leaves the flag false.

findings.where: A.5 rules 5 and 11; D.2 move_to_lab precondition, lease_cap come-home, run_replication come-home, restore_from_drive (target lab), evacuate_lab_to_drive; D.7 archive build
findings.problem: min_free_gb gates only 'a new job, download or archive'. The move_to_lab precondition, 'lab free disk ≥ (bytes that differ from the backup × 1.3)', ignores both floors. The automatic come-home paths (lease_cap with at_cap=come_home_if_lab_free, and run_replication) reuse that precondition. restore_from_drive to the lab has no disk precondition at all, yet it downloads parts into staging, unpacks beside them, and may need 'uv sync --frozen' (about 8 GB of CUDA wheels) if the venv was freed. evacuate_lab_to_drive, the emergency for a full disk, builds its tar --zstd parts on the lab disk first. Each of these can push the shared filesystem below the forge's 60 GB floor, which rule 11 forbids, and some do it automatically.
findings.scenario: Lab mates' growth leaves the shared disk at 61 GB free. A lease cap fires while the lab GPU is free. come_home_if_lab_free runs move_to_lab, the precondition (1.3 × 1.5 GB) passes, and free space falls to 59 GB. The forge hits its floor and stops its new work. This programme caused that, with no human involved.
findings.fix: Add to D.2, before the transitions: 'Every step that writes to the lab disk requires lab_free − bytes_to_write × 1.3 ≥ forge_floor_gb (60) + margin_gb (default 3). This covers move_to_lab, restore_from_drive to the lab, the come-home of lease_cap and run_replication, lab_mirror and lab-side archive builds. The check runs at the start and again before each writing step. If it fails, the transition is disabled with the numbers, and disk_floor offers Move to Vast or Evacuate.' D.7: build lab-side archives as a stream (tar | zstd -T8 | split with a filter that runs rclone rcat for each part), hashing each part in flight, so evacuation writes no scratch parts to the lab. Restore to the lab streams too (rclone cat for each part, through sha256sum and zstd -d | tar -x into staging) and runs the full verification afterwards.
findings.test: Model test on a fake filesystem at 61 GB free: move_to_lab of 2 GB and restore of 4 GB are refused with the reason, and the automatic come-home does not start. An evacuation at 60.5 GB free completes, writes no more than 100 MB to the lab (fake df), and verifies on the fake Drive.

findings.where: A.5 rule 5 (min_free_gb=65, hard_floor_gb=55); R.3 Disk; R.4 ('Only SAFE_PAUSE waits for a person'); N.10 disk_floor; 00_README 'Disk' default
findings.problem: A.4 and the probe measured 80-82 GB free, a figure that 'moves by tens of GB a day'. This programme's own install (a CUDA venv and the project caches, plausibly 8-10 GB) leaves about 5 GB of headroom above the 65 GB gate before the first job. The forge legitimately consumes space down to its 60 GB floor, so whenever free space sits in [60, 65), which the forge alone can cause, this programme starts nothing. Pipelines stall at every stage boundary, because each stage is a new job. Evacuating does not help: whatever this programme frees, the forge or lab mates can use until free space is back at 60. Below 55 GB, which lab mates alone can cause, SAFE_PAUSE waits for a person even after the disk recovers. This repeats A.2's failure: nothing runs while the user is away.
findings.scenario: On day 3 the forge's checkpoints settle free space at 62 GB. S1 of three campaign pipelines finishes and S2 never starts, and the dashboard shows 'idle, disk below floor' for days. A lab mate's 10 GB download briefly takes free space to 54 GB. SAFE_PAUSE fires, and the programme stays stopped overnight after the file is deleted.
findings.fix: In A.5 rule 5, replace 'it starts no new job, download or archive when the shared filesystem's free space is below min_free_gb = 65 GB' with: 'it starts a job, download or archive only if free − Σ(reserved-but-unwritten bytes of its running jobs) − the new item's declared max_disk_growth ≥ forge_floor_gb (60) + margin_gb (3). Each job kind declares max_disk_growth from its M1 measurements, and a job that exceeds its declaration by 25 % is stopped and re-queued. Checkpoint rotation that does not grow usage is always allowed.' Replace the disk trigger of SAFE_PAUSE with a self-clearing PAUSED(by: disk), which ends by itself once free ≥ hard_floor_gb + 5 has held for 30 minutes. Its disk_floor need is informational and offers Move to Vast (this frees CPU and GPU, not lab disk) and Evacuate (this frees disk). In Phase 0, if free space minus the install estimate is under 75 GB, raise a decision need quoting README question 5 (freeing part of ugrp-neurips-2027). These changes alter the user's README default, so present them to the user as a proposed change to accept.
findings.test: A 7-day simulation on a fake df: free space oscillates between 54 and 72 GB while a fake forge grows to its floor. The programme never writes below 63 GB, starts every job whose declared growth fits, never waits on a person for disk, and resumes within 35 minutes of recovery.

findings.where: R.2 'Host-resource fence' (admission rule, transient scopes, unit skeleton); C.5 admission; R.2 cold-start; D.2 polite_resume; H.7 sandbox queue; D.4 host view
findings.problem: The two programmes cannot deadlock on memory, because running jobs finish and free it. They can race, starve and kill each other. (1) Admission is a time-of-check-to-time-of-use race on one shared MemAvailable. A job's 32-48 environment processes spawn over seconds and allocate over tens of seconds (the probe saw MemAvailable fall from 23.0 to 19.7 GB for 32 processes). Both programmes, or two of this programme's own admissions, can pass 'stays above 6 GB' at once, and the two slices' MemoryMax sum to 39 GB against 30.8 GB of RAM. (2) The forge's worker runs with OOMScoreAdjust=600, Nice=10 and IOSchedulingClass=idle; the adaptation dropped all three for this worker. A global OOM therefore kills the forge's jobs first, even when this programme's growth caused it. (3) After a reboot both controllers start their workers within about a minute, and when a lab mate's job ends both programmes' polite pauses end at the same moment. Each is a stampede onto a MemAvailable that has not yet absorbed the other programme's ramp. (4) Sandbox trials start with no admission check at all. (5) Starvation: the forge's smaller jobs (6 GB scopes) re-admit whenever memory frees, while this programme's 8-12 GB jobs, whose environment count is a registered choice, can wait indefinitely behind only a generic idle alert. The host view already reads clforge.slice read-only, but admission does not use it.
findings.scenario: The lab reboots. Both workers resume at about t+90 s against 28 GB available. The forge admits two 6 GB jobs and this programme admits a 10 GB job, and all pass the check at once. Real usage climbs past physical RAM, and the kernel kills a forge job (adj 600) instead of this programme's (adj 0).
findings.fix: R.2: set OOMScoreAdjust=800, Nice=10 and IOSchedulingClass=idle on the worker unit, which job and sandbox scopes inherit, so this programme's jobs die before the forge's (600) and before lab mates' processes. The controller, bridge and watchdog stay at 0. Replace the admission sentence with: 'A job is admitted only if MemAvailable − Σ(declared − current RSS) over this programme's still-ramping jobs − forge_reserve − the new job's declared RAM ≥ 6 GB, where forge_reserve = min(4 GB, memory.max − memory.current of clforge.slice), read only from its cgroup files. After each admission the worker waits until the new job's RSS has stayed within 10 % for 60 s. After a boot_id change, a polite resume or any worker start, the first admission waits a random 2-6 minutes. Sandbox trials use the same rule. If queued work has waited only on memory for 2 h, the need memory_starved (registered in N.10) offers Move to Vast.' Phase 0: record whether systemd-oomd is active and what it would kill.
findings.test: With a fake /proc/meminfo and a fake clforge.slice cgroup, two admissions 1 s apart never both pass when together they would break the margin. A simulated 6 GB forge growth during this programme's ramp kills no forge job in the model. /proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj of an environment process reads 800. The cold-start drill passes with a fake forge ramp starting at the same time.

findings.where: A.5 rule 5 (same-account coexist); D.2 polite_pause (same_account_gpu: coexist | pause); C.5 GPU admission; R.3 GPU recoverable; R.5; B.5 throughput table; 00_README split ('GPU otherwise shared')
findings.problem: Each programme treats the other as a same-account process that coexists, so neither yields compute and no priority is defined. The probe saw the forge's training on the GPU at up to 93 % utilisation with about 2 GB held. After M4, MuJoCo Warp at 8,192 worlds saturates the GPU. Time-slicing then roughly halves both programmes, while the probe's 2.7× GPU advantage over 48 CPU processes assumed an otherwise idle GPU. GPU admission reads free memory with no reservation, so simultaneous admissions race. An out-of-memory that coincides with the other programme's growth is 'retried without a strike' with no bound or back-off: a possible livelock that pays Warp's roughly 62 s cold compile on each retry. The only knob, same_account_gpu=pause, pauses the whole worker, CPU work included, whenever llama-swap or open-webui loads a model. The user asked for a CPU, RAM and GPU split between the programmes that is visible and adjustable. For the GPU, this programme has no adjustable share of its own: only the sandbox has a VRAM cap.
findings.scenario: After M4 both programmes pack GPU jobs. A forge evaluation spikes to 6 GB exactly as this programme's 8,192-world job allocates. The job OOMs and is re-queued without a strike, then re-admitted 30 s later and OOMs again, dozens of times a day. Both programmes' throughput tables are measured on a contended GPU without saying so.
findings.fix: Keep coexist as the default (the user's 'GPU otherwise shared'), and add the missing mechanism. D.2 and A.5: same_account_gpu becomes coexist | yield_gpu_jobs | pause_all, offered to the user at M4 as a pick-one need with the measured contention figures. Under yield_gpu_jobs, no new GPU-backend job is admitted while a same-account process outside smatsprint.slice has used more than 50 % SM utilisation or 8 GB in 10 of the last 15 minutes (NVML per-process samples). Running GPU jobs finish their stage, CPU-backend jobs are unaffected, and after 6 h a need offers Move to Vast. Add the setting exp_vram_cap_gb (this programme's adjustable GPU share, shown in the host view beside the forge's live use). R.3 and R.5: no-strike re-queues after a coincident OOM back off for 5, 10, 20 … minutes, at most 6 per job per day, then raise gpu_contention (registered in N.10). The throughput table records whether the GPU was contended during each measurement.
findings.test: Fake NVML with a forge process at 93 %: under yield_gpu_jobs, GPU jobs wait and CPU jobs run. Seven coincident OOMs produce back-off and then the need, and never a strike. A throughput measurement taken while the fake forge is active is labelled contended. exp_vram_cap_gb limits the packer.

findings.where: A.5 rule 5 ('to a GPU and CPU free of this programme's processes'); D.1 GPU-free check (smatsprint-exp.slice only); D.2 pause, polite_pause, emergency_stop; H.7 sandbox runs and viewer; E.4 detach.sh --gpu-work
findings.problem: Pause, emergency stop and polite pause act only on the worker and smatsprint-exp.slice. Sandbox trial runs, renders and the viewer (up to 16 threads, 6 GB of RAM and 4 GB of VRAM) keep running. So do detached build jobs from detach.sh, whose slice is never specified, even though E.4 has M1's first Stage-1 runs and the throughput calibration run detached 'under the sprintctl pause'. The banner then says the GPU and CPU are verified free, which contradicts the rule-5 promise.
findings.scenario: A lab mate needs the GPU. Polite pause stops the experiment, but a 5-hour sandbox trial keeps 4 GB of VRAM and 16 cores until its idle stop, and the dashboard says the GPU is free of this programme's work. Or the user presses Pause during M4 while a detached parity job holds the GPU.
findings.fix: D.1 and D.2: 'Pause, emergency_stop and polite_pause stop every unit of this programme that can hold the GPU or burn CPU. That means smatsprint-exp.slice; sandbox runs and renders in smatsprint-sbx.slice (the viewer stays only if the setting pause_keeps_viewer=true, default false); and detached build jobs, which detach.sh --gpu-work always places in smatsprint-exp-build.slice, a child of the exp slice. The GPU-free check covers every PID whose cgroup is under smatsprint.slice, except the control slice and a permitted viewer. The banner names anything kept, for example: sandbox viewer still open, 0.6 GB.' Resume restarts only the experiment; stopped sandbox runs are restarted from their own Restart button.
findings.test: With a sandbox trial, the viewer and a detached GPU build job all running, Pause frees every PID within 60 s (the viewer too, by default). The GPU-free check fails while any of them holds the GPU. The polite-pause fixture also stops sandbox runs.

findings.where: D.3 'Fallback without GitHub' ('SSH plus sprintctl pause always works'); N.5 /pause; R.2 watchdog; R.3 harness bug; D.2 polite_pause, lease_cap
findings.problem: Every Pause path runs through the controller. The dashboard mailbox, Telegram /pause ('answered only after the controller acknowledges') and sprintctl ('writes the same command into the same queue') all depend on it. If the controller crash-loops (a bug, a corrupt state file, a bad release), nothing can pause the experiment, and polite mode, lease caps and disk floors go unenforced on the lab side. The watchdog timer only alerts. A manual 'systemctl --user stop smatsprint-worker.service' leaves the job scopes running (SM-01) and writes no desired.json. When the controller recovers, it reconciles 'LAB RUNNING' and restarts the worker, undoing the user's stop.
findings.scenario: A release introduces an exception in controller start-up, so the controller restarts every 10 s. A lab mate starts a GPU job and polite mode never fires. The watchdog's Gmail arrives, the user runs sprintctl pause over SSH, and the command sits in the queue while the GPU stays busy.
findings.fix: D.3: replace 'SSH plus sprintctl pause always works' with: 'sprintctl pause and sprintctl emergency-stop first queue the command. If the controller heartbeat is older than 60 s, or the command is not received within 30 s, they act directly. They write state/failsafe_pause.json {at, by, reason}, a file written only by this path, which the controller turns into PAUSED(by: user) on its next start and deletes once recorded. They then stop smatsprint-exp.slice (cgroup.kill for an emergency), and on VAST they write run=false over SSH and SIGTERM the recorded groups. The worker entry point and the Vast supervisor refuse to start while failsafe_pause.json exists.' R.2 watchdog: add 'when the controller has been silent for 15 minutes and either another account holds more than polite_min_mib on the GPU or a Vast lease has reached 100 % of its cap, the watchdog applies the same failsafe pause and alerts.' N.5: /pause falls back to the same path if the controller does not acknowledge within 60 s.
findings.test: Mask the controller (systemctl --user mask --runtime smatsprint-controller.service). sprintctl pause frees the slice within 60 s. With the controller still dead, a fake other-account GPU process triggers the watchdog's failsafe within 16 minutes. After unmasking, the phase is PAUSED(by: user or safe) and the worker is not restarted.

findings.where: D.2 polite_pause, polite_resume, resume ('or the user confirmed the override'); A.5 rule 5; move_to_lab step 6
findings.problem: (1) The forge's rule 'on confirm the loop runs and polite mode ignores the PIDs present at that moment' was dropped. After the user confirms Resume while a lab mate holds the GPU, polite_pause fires again within 60 s, so the override can never work. (2) Nothing damps flapping. A lab mate who runs short GPU jobs every 15 minutes causes a full pause and resume each time. Each cycle bumps the epoch and state_version, pays for the smoke and the environment spawn, and invalidates pending dashboard commands (SM-25). (3) 'Same account' is judged by service name ('the 11434 server'), but an Ollama-style server often runs as its own system user. By UID, which is what the rule says, that is another Linux account. (4) Before M4 the experiment may hold no GPU memory at all, and whether the trainer uses CUDA is unspecified. A polite pause then stops 48 cores of CPU physics to free a GPU it does not use. That is a legitimate choice, but it should be deliberate. (5) The state after a failed polite check at move_to_lab step 6 or at the automatic come-home is unspecified.
findings.scenario: A lab mate's notebook holds a 3 GB CUDA context all afternoon. The user taps Resume and confirms the override. 61 s later the experiment is paused again, and this repeats until the notebook closes.
findings.fix: D.2 resume: add 'On an override, the other accounts' GPU PIDs present at that moment are written to state/polite_ignore.json. Polite mode ignores them until they exit, and the dialog names them.' polite_resume: add 'After 3 polite pauses in 6 h, polite_resume_min doubles (cap 60 minutes); it resets after 24 h without one.' A.5 rule 5: classify by UID, not by service name. In Phase 0, record in docs/PLAN.md the UID behind each GPU process of llama-swap, open-webui and the 11434 server, and treat any UID other than aurnab as a lab mate. Add the setting polite_scope: all | gpu_jobs (default all, as the user wrote); the dialog explains that gpu_jobs keeps CPU physics running. move_to_lab and come-home end in PAUSED(by: polite) when the polite check fails, and polite_resume then applies.
findings.test: Fixture: a foreign 3 GB PID, then Resume with override. No polite pause occurs while that PID lives, and a new foreign PID does cause one. A fixture of 10 short foreign jobs an hour yields 3 pauses and then the doubled resume delay. A fake process with a non-aurnab UID above the threshold counts as a lab mate.

findings.where: A.5 rule 3; C.10; G.2 ('not comparable'); G.6 G1; G.8 (gate frozen in M1); D.6 offer choice; B.5 certificate; D.2 move_to_vast, run_replication
findings.problem: 'Hardware class' is never defined, yet gate/ freezes in M1, long before the M5 move semantics exercise it. Moves carry running jobs mid-stage to another host. Every cheap CPU host in the snapshot is AVX2-only (Xeon E5 v3/v4, EPYC Zen 2), while the lab's EPYC 9535 (Zen 5) has AVX-512. numpy, torch and oneDNN choose AVX-512 or AVX2 kernels at run time, so a resumed stage diverges in low-order bits: the job's class is undefined, and a paired block (C.6) can be split across classes. run_replication moves the whole queue, not only the replication cells. The GPU certificate (backend id, model hash, versions, code_id, parity report) names no device, so a CPU-heavy offer's small GPU (A16, T4, RTX 3060, 5060 Ti in the snapshot) would run GPU-backend jobs under the lab 5090's certificate. Offer choice happens once per move, while the queue mixes CPU and GPU jobs.
findings.scenario: Q5's paired controls (B0, B2, B4 and A2-A4 on the same S2 seeds) are half done when the user moves to a USD 0.33/h 128-core EPYC 7V12 host, and the remaining arms finish there. The gate then either counts a cross-class comparison silently, or declares a day of compute 'not comparable' with no warning before the move. Separately, a queued GPU-backend Stage-1 job runs on that host's RTX 5070 Ti under the lab certificate.
findings.fix: Before gate/ freezes, add to gate/criteria.yaml and C.10: 'Hardware class for CPU-physics jobs = (ISA level avx512 or avx2; the mujoco, numpy and torch wheel versions). For GPU-backend jobs = (compute capability, driver major, warp and mujoco-warp versions). A job's class is the set of classes its stages ran on; a job spanning two classes is mixed and not comparable in any paired block.' D.2 move_to_vast and run_replication: 'The dialog lists every paired block with a stage in progress and offers Drain first (about N h: running stages finish on the lab and nothing new is delivered) or Move now (those blocks become not comparable and are re-queued from their branch checkpoint). run_replication delivers only the claim's replication cells to Vast; everything else waits in the outbox.' D.6: 'For CPU work, prefer offers in the lab's ISA class. Choose the offer for the next 12 h of the queue: 5090-class when it holds certified GPU-backend work.' B.5: 'The certificate includes the GPU class. The controller delivers a GPU-backend job only to a host whose GPU matches a valid certificate.'
findings.test: Gate synthetic ledgers: a paired arm whose S3 ran on both lab and Vast is not comparable, and a certificate from sm_120 is invalid on sm_75. Delivery fake: a GPU job is never delivered to a T4 host. Model test: the move dialog lists exactly the paired blocks in progress.

findings.where: R.2 ('On Vast there is no systemd; the thread caps and the host-RAM admission rule still apply'); C.5 admission; D.6 ranking (transitions/s ÷ dph_total); D.2 lab_mirror ('120 when the offer charges for bandwidth')
findings.problem: Inside a Docker container, /proc/meminfo, MemAvailable and os.cpu_count() describe the whole host. The snapshot includes 256-core hosts that sell 32 effective cores, and one host with 515.6 GB of RAM. A worker applying the lab rules unchanged packs by host RAM and host cores. It then oversubscribes its cgroup and hits the container OOM killer, or runs 48 environment processes on 32 paid cores. The ranking divides by dph_total, which prices storage at the CLI's 5 GiB default (vast-03, vast-08), not the 60 GB disk requested; at USD 0.13-0.60 per GB-month that is roughly 10 % of the price. Bandwidth, 500 times dearer on some hosts, is left out of the ranking. Every snapshot offer charges something for bandwidth, so 'charges for bandwidth' is undefined.
findings.scenario: On a 256-core EPYC 7B12 host selling 32 effective cores and about 64 GB, the worker sees 256 CPUs and hundreds of GB of MemAvailable. It packs three 48-environment jobs, and the container OOM killer takes the supervisor.
findings.fix: R.2, Vast bullet: 'On Vast the worker takes its budgets from the container. CPU = min(cpu.max quota / period, the affinity mask size, the offer's cpu_cores_effective). RAM = cgroup memory.max − memory.current (v2 or v1 paths), falling back to the lease's cpu_ram. It never uses /proc/meminfo or os.cpu_count() there. The 6 GB margin applies to that figure. Jobs run with oom_score_adj 900, so the container OOM killer takes them before the supervisor and the guard (0).' D.6: 'Search with --storage <requested disk GB> so that dph_total includes real storage. Rank by transitions/s ÷ (dph_total + expected GB per day × (inet_up_cost + inet_down_cost) / 24), counting the move in, mirrors, record pulls and the move out. The Move dialog shows the bandwidth share. An offer charges for bandwidth when inet_up_cost > USD 0.01/GB.'
findings.test: A fake container with cpu.max '3200000 100000' and memory.max 32G, on a host reporting 256 CPUs and 515 GB: the worker runs at most 32 environment threads and admits within 26 GB. A ranking unit test on the 2026-09-23 snapshot at a 60 GB disk gives the expected order. The M5 rehearsal records the container's cgroup files in its report.

findings.where: C.2 run trees (git archive by the worker); D.1 delivery rule; D.2 move_to_vast step 4; D.6 Image; R.5 ('a missing code tree' is an infrastructure event); R.9 release; R.10
findings.problem: The worker materialises each job's code with 'git archive <sha>', but a Vast worker has no git objects, and R.10 forbids pulling code from anywhere but the lab. Code reaches Vast only at provisioning and during the move ('the code from the lab's archive'). The adaptation dropped the forge's D.1 rule: 'before delivering, the controller makes sure the job's code tree is on the worker; a job whose code is missing goes back to the outbox without a strike'. After any sprintctl release that changes code_id, or any candidate registered on newer code while the work is on Vast, each such job fails on the missing code tree, is re-queued without a strike and is re-delivered, forever.
findings.scenario: While the work is on Vast, the user drains, a Codex session releases svc-7 with a trainer fix, and the user resumes. Every new candidate's jobs bounce between the outbox and Vast, and the dashboard shows nothing but a queue that never moves.
findings.fix: D.1, after 'The controller is the only process that delivers jobs': 'Before delivering a job to Vast, the controller ensures work/code/<code_id>/ and its venv exist there. It builds git archive <sha> smatsprint eval uv.lock on the lab and rsyncs it into code/<code_id>.staging with its sha256. It then verifies it, renames it into place, and runs uv sync --frozen --no-install-project there as a polled child. Only then does it deliver. A job whose code is not on the worker yet stays in the outbox with the reason waiting for code on the worker. The worker never runs git on Vast. Missing-code re-queues are capped at 3 per job per hour, then raise unexpected.' C.2: 'on Vast the run tree comes only from the controller's shipment'.
findings.test: Fake Vast host without git: after a release, the new code_id is shipped once and hash-verified, and its jobs then run. Delivery refuses until the code verifies. A deliberately corrupted archive is rejected and never delivered.

findings.where: A.5 rule 6; D.2 move_to_vast precondition and lease_cap ('the monthly cap', 'credit at the floor'); D.6 'Lease and billing'; D.3 limits.toml
findings.problem: The Vast account 'UGRP Exp' is shared with the forge (also USD 150 a month) and with other people. The spec never says what 'the monthly cap' counts. An implementation that reads account-level charges throttles this programme by the forge's spending. One that counts only this programme's leases lets the two programmes spend USD 300 against a budget the user may have meant as one. The credit is shared too. Both programmes' floors (USD 5) and the 'credit ≥ floor + 2 h of the offer's price' precondition are checked independently, so both can rent on the same small balance. At zero balance Vast stops every instance on the account, including teammates' instances and a parked instance still billing storage. A 2-hour margin also allows a futile cycle: rent, provision, copy, then come home immediately.
findings.scenario: The forge moves to Vast on Monday with USD 30 of credit. On Tuesday this programme's precondition passes with USD 6 left (5 + 2 × 0.33). Within hours both programmes hit the floor and park or come home, and a teammate's unrelated instance is stopped at zero balance.
findings.fix: A.5 rule 6: add 'The monthly cap counts only this programme's spend: the billed cost, in the UTC calendar month, of all its lease records, open and closed, whose label starts with smatsprint-. An M5 need asks the user once whether USD 150 is this programme's own cap or a budget shared with the forge. If shared, the effective cap is 150 minus the forge's month-to-date spend, read-only from instances labelled ugrp-forge- and never acted on.' D.2 move_to_vast precondition: 'credit ≥ credit_floor_usd (default 20) + max_usd of the new lease + storage for parked_destroy_after_h. The credit is re-read immediately before the create call.' D.6: 'When credit ≤ floor + 2 h of the dph of every instance on the account, park this programme's instance and raise vast_credit_low; at zero balance Vast stops every instance on the account.' The dashboard shows the account's month-to-date spend by label prefix, read-only.
findings.test: Fake Vast with USD 140 of forge-labelled spend this month: this programme's cap is untouched when separate and USD 10 when shared. A create by another label between the check and the create is caught by the re-read. At low credit, this programme's instance is parked before the balance reaches zero.

findings.where: D.7 (own rclone config; 'Space first'; 'keep the two newest verified archives'); D.2 evacuate_lab_to_drive, backup_to_drive; N.7 Google Drive; README M6 row
findings.problem: (1) One full lab disk triggers both programmes' emergency evacuations at once, and both draw on one Google quota: 15 GB on a free account, shared with Gmail and Photos. Each programme checks the free space for itself, so the two uploads collide mid-transfer. (2) drive.file grants belong to the app, which is its Google Cloud project. If the user creates this programme's OAuth client inside the forge's project, either token can see the other's archives, and the M6 need does not require a separate project. (3) The forge kept 'never prune an archive that holds a base checkpoint or a cache key absent from the newer ones'; the adaptation keeps only 'the two newest verified archives'. Consider: a full archive, then an evacuation that deletes the lab files it holds, then two lean archives. The full archive is pruned, and the stage-final checkpoints of candidates below L1, which lean archives omit, are lost. That breaks 'nothing is deleted before its replacement copy is verified'.
findings.scenario: On a Friday night the shared disk reaches 58 GB. The forge and this programme both start evacuating. Both see 9 GB free on Drive, both start 5-6 GB uploads, and both fail at part 3 with 'quota exceeded'. This programme's emergency path fails exactly when it is needed.
findings.fix: D.7: add 'This programme's Google Cloud project is separate from the forge's; the M6 need says so. A lean backup_to_drive runs daily at 04:00 KST when Drive has room, so an emergency evacuation usually finds a verified archive newer than what it deletes and needs no upload. An upload starts only if Drive free space ≥ 1.5 × the estimated size. A quota error re-reads rclone about and raises drive_quota_low with the numbers instead of retrying blindly.' Replace 'keep the two newest verified archives' with: 'keep the two newest verified archives, and never prune an archive that holds a file whose lab copy an evacuation deleted and that no newer verified archive holds. Each MANIFEST.json records which of its files were later evacuated from the lab.'
findings.test: Two fake programmes sharing one fake Drive quota: this programme's evacuation either completes or fails before deleting anything, and raises the need. The sequence full archive, evacuate, lean, lean never prunes the full archive while it holds the only copy of a file. The M6 checklist requires a separate Cloud project.

findings.where: A.5 rule 6; D.6 renting and rehearsals; I10; R.7 reconciliation; E.2 migration rehearsal; D.3 sprintctl subcommands
findings.problem: The rehearsal label smatsprint-rehearsal-* lies inside the production prefix smatsprint-, and the rehearsal runs 'from its own checkout with its own state/ root'. Each controller therefore sees the other's instance under its own prefix with no lease. The forge's R.7 rule for exactly this case ('without a lease … is reported, and nothing is destroyed automatically') was dropped. What remains is 'orphans with no worker ever started are destroyed', which an implementation can read as 'no lease means no worker'. 'At most one billable instance with the prefix' also makes each block the other. The forge restricted forgectl destroy-labelled to the rehearsal prefix; sprintctl destroy-labelled has no restriction at all. On a shared account, one typo (smatsprint- or ugrp-forge-), or a wrong argument to the dead-man switch, destroys instances without any I2 check.
findings.scenario: The M5 rehearsal runs while production is on Vast. The rehearsal's controller reconciles, finds smatsprint-<lease_id> with no lease in its own state root, treats it as an orphan, and destroys the production instance along with its unmirrored work.
findings.fix: D.6: 'Production labels are smatsprint-prod-<lease_id>; rehearsal labels are smatsprint-reh-<id>. Each controller instance acts only on its configured prefix, and production treats smatsprint-reh- as foreign.' Restore in R.7: 'An instance under this programme's prefix without a lease, or a lease without an instance, is reported and never destroyed automatically. Reconciliation destroys only an instance whose own lease shows that no worker ever started.' D.3: 'sprintctl destroy-labelled accepts only the hard-coded rehearsal prefix. Any other argument is refused and logged before any API call. It never destroys an instance whose lease shows a worker start.'
findings.test: Model test: with a rehearsal instance present, production reconciliation reports it and neither adopts nor destroys it, and the reverse holds too. sprintctl destroy-labelled smatsprint- and sprintctl destroy-labelled ugrp-forge- both exit non-zero, and the fake Vast records no API call.

findings.where: C.5 (checkpoint at every PPO update boundary, keep the last two); D.2 lab_mirror, backup_to_drive, the no-room Drive refresh; D.7
findings.problem: At B.7's planning rate of about 20,000 end-to-end transitions per second, one 65,536-transition SMAT update takes roughly 3-5 s per job. With 'keep the last two', a checkpoint therefore lives only about 6-10 s. The mirror fetches latest and then rsyncs the listed files over a WAN, so files are routinely rotated away mid-transfer. The adaptation dropped the forge's rule 'rsync exit 23 or 24 means the worker rotated: re-read latest and retry once'. It also dropped the rule that the mirror's age is the oldest run's verified checkpoint, stamped only when every run passed. backup_to_drive on a RUNNING lab, and the 6-hourly Drive refresh from Vast, tar a tree whose files disappear every few seconds. Nothing pins a consistent snapshot.
findings.scenario: On Vast with 4 packed jobs, about a third of mirror attempts per run fail with vanished files. The banner shows 'backup: Lab (12 min old)', taken from the one run that succeeded, while two runs' newest verified lab checkpoint is 3 hours old. A host loss then costs 3 hours, not the 30 minutes the banner implies.
findings.fix: C.5: add a pin protocol: 'On runs/<id>/ckpt/pin_request (written over SSH on Vast), at the next update boundary the worker hard-links the files of latest into ckpt/pinned/<epoch>-<update>/ with their manifest and writes pin_ready. Retention never deletes a pinned set before pin_release.' D.2 lab_mirror, backup_to_drive and the Drive refresh: 'copy only pinned sets'. Restore the forge's rules: 'rsync exit 23 or 24 on a listed file: re-read latest and retry that run once', and 'copies.lab_backup.kind=mirror is stamped only when every unfinished run passed; its age is the oldest run's verified checkpoint'.
findings.test: A fake worker rotating checkpoints every 2 s passes 100 mirror cycles with every run verified. backup_to_drive of a RUNNING lab produces an archive whose manifest verifies. The banner's age equals the oldest run's verified checkpoint.

findings.where: R.2 (smatsprint-ctl.slice CPUQuota=200%, MemoryMax=1G; 'Bulk work is polite'); N.8 (Codex sessions in smatsprint-ctl.slice); C.13 summaries; D.7 archive builds
findings.problem: The latency-critical controller shares a 1 GB, 2-CPU slice with the runner, bridge, wrapper and watchdog. N.8 also places every Codex build session there (codex exec, pytest importing MuJoCo and torch, uv sync). So do the controller's bulk children (rsync, tar | zstd -T8, rclone, uv sync --frozen for restores) and C.13's codex exec summaries. A build session alone exceeds 1 GB, so the memory cgroup's OOM killer fires inside the slice and may pick the controller or the runner. Compression and tests compete with the controller loop for 2 CPUs, which threatens the ≤ 60 s Pause target, the watchdog heartbeats and the no-blocking rule.
findings.scenario: During M3 a Codex session runs the lanes fuzzer, which imports torch and MuJoCo in several processes. The ctl slice reaches 1 GB and the OOM killer takes the controller. Restart=always brings it back after 10 s plus reconciliation, and a Pause sent 20 s earlier is acknowledged 2 minutes late.
findings.fix: R.2 slice table: 'smatsprint-ctl.slice holds only the controller, runner, bridge, wrapper and watchdog: MemoryMax=2G, MemoryLow=768M, CPUQuota=400%. smatsprint-build.slice holds Codex sessions and detached CPU build jobs: MemoryMax=6G, CPUQuota=800%, OOMScoreAdjust=900, admitted by the 6 GB rule before launch. smatsprint-bulk.slice holds rsync, tar/zstd, rclone, uv sync and summary calls: MemoryMax=2G, CPUQuota=800%, Nice=15, idle I/O; they run as transient units started with --slice=smatsprint-bulk.slice --collect and are polled.' N.8: the session command uses --slice=smatsprint-build.slice. smatsprint.slice's MemoryMax becomes a sum the user approves, and admission, not static caps, coordinates (R.2).
findings.test: With a fake Codex session allocating 4 GB and a zstd -T8 archive build running, press Pause. It verifies within 60 s, and the journal shows no OOM kill or watchdog kill of the controller, runner or bridge.

findings.where: D.3 'Dashboard auth' ('Shared origin … the forge's dashboard will join it'); D.4 LAST KNOWN banner; E.2 Dashboard group
findings.problem: Both dashboards are Pages sites on mushfique-dgist.github.io and share one localStorage, and this programme's shell is copied from the forge's. PIN encryption protects confidentiality, not key names. If the token, the device-expiry date or the cached last-good status.json use the same keys, each page overwrites the other's token, and the LAST KNOWN banner can show the other programme's state. That happens during an outage, exactly when the banner matters. A service worker registered at the origin root by either page would also intercept the other page's requests.
findings.scenario: The user opens the forge's dashboard, then this one. This page cannot decrypt the forge's token with its own PIN and asks for a token, the user pastes it, and now the forge's page asks again: ping-pong on the phone. During a GitHub outage, this page's stale banner shows the forge's cached 'RUNNING on Vast'.
findings.fix: D.3: 'Every localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB and Cache Storage key is prefixed with the repository name (smat-sprint-lab:). The page registers no service worker, and it ignores, and never deletes, keys without its prefix.' Add to E.2 Dashboard: a two-dashboard test.
findings.test: Playwright: serve the forge's shell and this one from one fake origin under two paths. Log in to both and reload each 10 times. Both tokens survive, each banner shows only its own cached status, and neither page reads or writes the other's keys.

findings.where: R.3 'GPU, recoverable' ('retry once with the next smaller declared world count, flagged in the row'); B.5 ('A different rollout geometry is a registered choice, never silently swapped'); C.3 job identity; C.6 paired blocks
findings.problem: The automatic out-of-memory fallback changes a registered choice (the world count, and with it the batch geometry) while the job keeps its identity. That contradicts B.5 and the matched-comparison rule of C.10. The row is flagged, but nothing in Part G stops a flagged arm from counting toward a paired comparison or a claim.
findings.scenario: After M4 a Stage-4 arm runs out of memory because the forge grew, and the coincidence check misses it. The job retries at 4,096 worlds instead of 8,192 and finishes, and its paired block is judged as matched.
findings.fix: R.3: replace 'otherwise retry once with the next smaller declared world count, flagged in the row' with 'otherwise re-queue unchanged, and admit it only when free GPU memory exceeds its declaration by 20 %. A second out-of-memory at that margin is a strike with the reason declared GPU memory too small. A smaller world count is a new registered version through the steering API (B.5).'
findings.test: Fake CUDA out-of-memory: the retried job keeps the same config hash and world count. A synthetic gate ledger in which one arm's world count differs from its registration fails G1.

findings.where: C.1 controller ('It polls commands'); D.1 Pause target; D.2 drain; D.5 signals; I4
findings.problem: The forge's poll interval ('git ls-remote origin refs/heads/control' every 15 s) was dropped, so the ≤ 90 s button-to-free budget has no stated input. drain says running jobs 'finish their current PPO update and checkpoint', but D.5 defines only SIGTERM, which drops the partial rollout, and SIGUSR1, which checkpoints and continues. No signal means 'finish this update, then exit'. I4 ('at most one PPO update') is undefined for eval, ctrl_tune, render, throughput and parity jobs; a B3 or B4 ctrl_tune grid can run for hours without an update boundary.
findings.scenario: The implementation polls control every 60 s. A phone Pause then takes up to 60 s of poll wait plus about 50 s of stop plus the verification reads, and fails the M2 acceptance line. Separately, a drained ctrl_tune job restarts its whole grid.
findings.fix: C.1: 'The controller polls git ls-remote origin refs/heads/control every 15 s and the local queue every 1 s.' D.5: 'desired.json gains drain: true, sent with SIGUSR2. Each job finishes its current PPO update (or grid point, or evaluation batch), checkpoints and exits 0 with the reason drained.' I4: 'resume loses at most one PPO update of a training job, one grid point of a ctrl_tune job and one evaluation batch of an eval job; render, throughput and parity jobs restart.'
findings.test: The M2 phone test logs GitHub latency, poll wait and stop time separately. A drained PPO job's parameters equal the uninterrupted twin's at that update. A drained ctrl_tune job resumes at its next grid point.

findings.where: D.3 'Ordering and staleness'; H.5 ('carries based_on (the state_version the sender saw)'); D.2 state_version; N.5 buttons
findings.problem: state_version increments on every change of phase kind, so every polite pause and resume bumps it. Steering actions carry state_version as based_on, and D.3 rejects a state-changing command whose based_on differs. Queue edits made from the dashboard are then rejected for reasons unrelated to the queue. So is Move to Vast from a polite_pause_long message once one more polite cycle has passed.
findings.scenario: A lab mate's jobs cause 5 polite cycles in an afternoon. The user reorders the queue twice and adds seeds from the phone, and every action is rejected with 'the state changed'.
findings.fix: D.3 and H.5: 'Queue and candidate steering actions carry based_on_queue (the runner's queue version) and the version of the candidate they edit. They are rejected only when those have changed; location and phase changes never reject them. A command sent from a need's button carries the need's nonce and stays valid while the need is open.'
findings.test: During 5 fake polite cycles, 20 queue edits from a stale page all apply. An edit against a candidate version that has changed is rejected with a plain message.

findings.where: D.2 I2 (unreachable clause); D.2 'Replace = fence first'
findings.problem: An instance that the API reports as running but that SSH cannot reach (direct and proxy) for 15 minutes is treated as lost and destroyed. A cause on the lab side looks exactly the same: campus egress policy blocking outbound SSH while HTTPS to the Vast API still works, or a DNS or tailnet fault. A healthy instance would then be destroyed, together with up to mirror_interval (30-120 minutes) of work not yet mirrored.
findings.scenario: The campus firewall blocks outbound high ports for an hour. Both SSH paths fail while the API says the instance is running, and at minute 15 the controller destroys it.
findings.fix: I2 and Replace: 'The 15 minutes count only while a lab-side SSH canary succeeds (ssh -T git@github.com with the deploy key, plus a TCP connect to a second host behind the same Vast proxy). While the canary also fails, the fault is the lab's network: no fence, an alert, and the lease clock keeps running.'
findings.test: Fake: block the lab's SSH egress for 30 minutes. There is no destroy, an alert is sent, and after unblocking the instance is reachable and reconciled.

findings.where: D.8 deadman.yml; R.8 doctor ('the last run of the off-lab dead-man workflow')
findings.problem: After M2 the lab holds only the deploy key, which works only for git. The workflow has contents: read, and the dashboard token is limited to Contents. Nothing can read the workflow's runs, so the doctor's line cannot be implemented, and a disabled or failing dead-man goes unnoticed. The forge's and this programme's hourly jobs each bill about 744 minutes a month (a 1-minute minimum per job) against the account's private-repository Actions allowance, which is 3,000 minutes on Pro.
findings.scenario: The account runs out of Actions minutes on the 20th, or scheduled runs stop silently. The lab dies on the 25th and no issue ever opens.
findings.fix: D.8: 'The workflow (timeout-minutes: 2, contents: write) also force-pushes one commit with its run time to a deadman branch, which ruleset A excludes. The controller fetches that branch with the deploy key, and the doctor alerts when it is older than 3 h.' docs/USER_ACTIONS.md records the Actions minutes both programmes use.
findings.test: After the deliberate M2 firing, the doctor shows the deadman branch as less than 1 h old. A stale fake branch turns the doctor red and sends an alert.

findings.where: N.5 'Conflicts and outages'; R.2 watchdog ('Gmail if the bridge itself is the silent one'); R.8 doctor
findings.problem: Gmail is the bridge's fallback, and it is the watchdog's only path when the bridge is silent. It depends on another project's files (~/.config/dgist-agents/{menu,notice}/service.env) and on their app password. The doctor checks the bridge but never SMTP, so a rotated password or a moved file is discovered only when Telegram or the bridge is already down.
findings.scenario: The DGIST agents rotate their Gmail app password in October. In November the bridge crash-loops, the watchdog's mail fails with error 535, and the user hears nothing until the 45-minute dead-man fires, and that fires only if the whole lab is silent.
findings.fix: R.8 doctor: 'Daily, check the Gmail fallback without sending: the five variables are present, then SMTP connect, STARTTLS and AUTH within 30 s. Weekly, send one test mail. On failure, raise a Telegram need while Telegram still works.' The watchdog and the bridge use the same code path.
findings.test: A fake SMTP server that rejects AUTH turns the doctor red and raises the need. A fake SMTP server that accepts receives exactly one weekly test mail.

findings.where: A.4 tools ('Reuse the binaries; never reuse their configurations'); A.5 rule 5 cache list; N.7 gh version pin; D.6 vastai; N.8 builder forbidden rules
findings.problem: gh, rclone, vastai and uv are called from ~/.local/bin, where the forge's build installed them and can upgrade them at any time. This programme parses gh's device-code output ('display output, not a stable interface') and vastai's output, so a forge upgrade silently changes what it reads, possibly in the middle of a rental. CUDA_CACHE_PATH and PYTHONPYCACHEPREFIX are missing from rule 5's cache list. CUDA JIT output therefore lands in the shared ~/.nv/ComputeCache, which the probe deliberately avoided and flagged as shared. The builder's forbidden rules cover stop, restart and disable, but not set-property, kill, mask, reset-failed or daemon-reexec on the forge's units and slices.
findings.scenario: A forge session upgrades vastai to fix one of its own problems. This programme's parsing of 'show instances' breaks and NO_VAST opens, while its rental keeps billing until the guard's thresholds stop it.
findings.fix: A.4: 'Install pinned copies of gh, rclone, vastai and uv under ~/.local/share/smatsprint/bin/. Check their sha256 at every start and in the doctor, and never call ~/.local/bin/{gh,rclone,vastai,uv}.' A.5 rule 5: add CUDA_CACHE_PATH and PYTHONPYCACHEPREFIX to the list of project caches. N.8: turn the systemctl --user rule into an allow-list: any verb on smatsprint-* units and slices; elsewhere only show, status, list-units, is-active and daemon-reload.
findings.test: A grep test finds no ~/.local/bin/(gh|rclone|vastai|uv) path in the tree. The doctor fails when a pinned binary's hash changes. An environment test asserts that CUDA_CACHE_PATH lies under <project>/cache/.

strengths: The controller stays the single source of truth. desired.json is written and fsynced before any signal. The worker unit is never enabled, so systemd can neither undo a Pause nor start the worker after a reboot. A cold-start drill replaces reboots, and a boot_id change is logged as a real drill.

GPU ownership is decided by process, not by memory level, and other people's memory is reported in words. Pause is explicitly extended to CPU cores, which is the right goal for a CPU-physics programme; SM-01 fixes the mechanism.
Fence-first replacement, 'an instance the API reports as stopped is never lost', at most one open lease, and idempotent adopt-before-create renting under a lease-id label are all carried over intact.

Non-interference with the forge is explicit and mostly concrete. Label prefixes are disjoint (smatsprint- versus ugrp-forge-), ports are separate (8800-8809 versus 8790-8799), and so are the bots, secrets directories and rclone configs. GH_CONFIG_DIR is used with --insecure-storage, which catches the shared GNOME-keyring collision. The builder has forbidden-command guardrails, the server is never rebooted, and the floors are chosen so this programme is never the reason the forge reaches its 60 GB floor.

Admission, not static caps, is named as the real coordination between two programmes whose caps together exceed the machine. The host view shows both programmes read-only, and each programme adjusts only its own share.

Interruptible offers are forbidden because they would break I4 without warning. The offer's end date is acted on 6 h ahead. The first job on a new host checks physics parity. Offers are ranked by measured transitions per dollar, with the first job's measured rate replacing the estimate.

The rehearsal budget is USD 5 or less, with its own dead-man destroy switch. It checks the four unknowns that matter: the guard's self-stop with the lab link blocked, the instance key's scope, copying from a stopped instance, and whether nvidia-smi lists PIDs inside the container.
Checkpoints at every PPO update boundary make I4 strong and cheap here, because the networks are small. Checkpoints are never pickles, and everything returning from a rented host is untrusted data.

The state machine is a pure function with fakes and model-based testing. Pause, cancel and emergency stop are injected at every step, and a partitioned instance returning after replacement and a create call that times out after succeeding are both covered.
Several alert paths are independent of each other: an off-lab dead-man workflow that holds no secrets, a Gmail fallback, and a watchdog that shares no code with the controller.
